bridge: Builds on C04 pointer lifetime, C05 machine execution and C02 bounds. This exercise is a memory-layout model; do not execute invalid memory accesses.
teaching:
Memory corruption violates the intended boundaries or lifetime of an object. A write beyond an array may affect adjacent data; a use-after-free accesses an object after its lifetime ends. The visible consequence depends on layout, compiler and runtime, so one crash pattern is not the definition of the defect.

Reason from source-level cause to affected invariant. If an array has capacity 4 and a routine writes 5 bytes, the bounds violation exists even if the adjacent byte happens to be unused in one build. An exploitability claim needs additional evidence about reachable input, layout and protections. Do not equate every crash with arbitrary code execution.

The repair should remove the invalid operation and preserve valid inputs. Use capacity-aware interfaces, explicit ownership and memory-safe representations where possible. Sanitizers can reveal classes of invalid access during tests, but a clean test run does not prove every path safe.
example:
Abstract memory (not an actual compiler layout)
index: 0 1 2 3 | adjacent object
array: A B C 0 | flag=0
capacity4 includes terminator.
Attempt to store "ABCDE" plus terminator needs6 bytes.
Root cause: required size6 exceeds capacity4.
Repair policy: reject input; do not perform a partial unsafe write.
explanation: The 0 in the array is the zero-valued terminating byte, not the printable digit "0". Five ASCII letters plus that byte need 6 slots. The model makes the arithmetic visible without relying on a platform-specific layout; the neighbouring flag is illustrative, not a promise about an actual C stack. Reject before copying. If you checked only after copying, the invalid write would already have happened.
exercise: For capacity 8, calculate required bytes for ASCII strings of lengths 0,7,8 and12 with a terminator. Classify accepted/rejected inputs under a no-truncation policy. State a separate lifetime defect not captured by this capacity check.
solution: Add one terminating byte: lengths 0, 7, 8 and 12 require 1, 8, 9 and 13 bytes. With capacity 8 and no truncation, accept lengths 0 and 7; reject 8 and 12 before writing. Capacity and lifetime are different: a pointer to an already freed 8-byte allocation is invalid even for a one-byte access.
challenge: Write a root-cause report for a hypothetical copy of 10 bytes into an8-byte object. Separate proven bounds failure, possible consequences and evidence still needed before claiming exploitability.
challenge_solution: Proven in the model: writing 10 bytes into an 8-byte object exceeds capacity by 2, violating the bounds invariant. Possible effects include corrupted adjacent data, a crash or control-flow impact, but the packet does not prove which occurs. Needed evidence includes input reachability, actual layout, first invalid access and applicable protections. Repair the size/lifetime contract and test required sizes 7, 8 and 9: first two fit this 8-byte object, the last rejects.
